sources.text: For studying, exams, finals, homework, reading, or any task that needs concentration and focus. Many listeners find lyrics distracting while they read or write, so steady music with low vocal intensity and relatively low energy is a common choice for study sessions. Relevant features: energy, instrumentalness, vocal intensity, the `focused` mood tag. May not apply: some people concentrate better with familiar songs that have lyrics, or with upbeat music that keeps them awake. Studying does **not** imply a particular genre; the assistant never assumes lofi just because someone is studying.
sources.title: Studying and concentration

sources.text: Vocal intensity is a 0 to 1 estimate of how prominent and forceful the vocals are. Low values suit background or study listening; high values suit sing-along or performance-driven songs. It is only scored when advanced scoring is on.
sources.title: Vocal intensity

sources.text: Instrumentalness is a 0 to 1 estimate of how much of a song has no vocals. High values suit requests for instrumental music, music without lyrics, or music without distracting vocals. It is only scored when advanced scoring is on.
sources.title: Instrumentalness

sources.text: Genre describes a song's style (rock, lofi, jazz). Mood describes how it feels (happy, chill, sad). A rock song can be moody and a pop song can be intense, so the two are scored separately. Labels match exactly after case and spacing are normalized: "indie pop" does not count as "pop". When a listener names several genres ("rock or hip-hop"), a song matching any of them earns the single genre contribution once.
